sketch: Instead of simulating Shor's circuit under sampled gate-error models, build a tiny order-finding instance (N=15, a=7, order r=4) with the semiclassical-free, unitary form: counting register of t=4 qubits, work register of 4 qubits. Steps: (1) prepare |0>^t|1>; (2) Hadamards on counting qubits; (3) controlled modular multiplication by a^(2^j) mod N compiled as permutation gates (explicit classical parameters a, N compiled into gates); (4) inverse QFT built from H and controlled-phase gates CP(-pi/2^k). Imperfection is introduced as a deterministic perturbation of each controlled-phase angle in the inverse QFT: theta_k -> theta_k(1+epsilon_k). Systematic error: epsilon_k = epsilon constant. Random error: epsilon_k drawn i.i.d. from a zero-mean distribution with variance sigma^2 (compiled as fixed sampled angles per circuit instance). Combined: both. The claim is assessed analytically through the fidelity F = |<psi_ideal|psi_err>|^2 of the final state, or the probability mass on peaks near multiples of 2^t/r. A systematic rotation error is a coherent unitary deformation that largely rescales phases consistently, shifting peak positions slightly without destroying them, so the success probability degrades smoothly (robust). Random errors add incoherent-like phase noise per gate, so infidelity accumulates as roughly sum of variances proportional to the number of gates G ~ O(L^3) with L=log2 N, giving F ≈ exp(-G sigma^2). The threshold is the sigma_c where the success probability falls below a chosen level, e.g. sigma_c ~ 1/sqrt(G) scaling with N via L. Postprocessing: measure counting register, continued fractions to get r, then gcd(a^(r/2)±1, N). The circuit is only a tiny N=15 unitary with measurement removed; decoding of the counting register is done classically.
